description:
The stranger, truer version: that veto only existed on his boat because of where he happened to be standing. The other submarines in the same group didn't need his agreement at all.

Cornered by US Navy destroyers off Cuba, out of radio contact with Moscow for days, carrying a nuclear torpedo with roughly the power of the Hiroshima bomb.

They dropped practice depth charges as a signal, not to sink it. Nobody aboard B-59 knew that. They didn't know if the war outside had already started.

Two said yes. The third was Vasily Arkhipov, the flotilla's chief of staff, who happened to be riding that particular submarine. On the other three boats in the group, only two signatures were needed, his rank was the only reason B-59 required three.

How long the story stayed buried, first acknowledged at a 1997 Moscow conference, fully confirmed at a 2002 Havana conference where both sides compared notes for the first time.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_submarine_B-59: read. Establishes B-59 (a Foxtrot-class submarine, one of four in a detachment with B-4, B-36 and B-130) was cornered by US Navy ships including USS Cony and USS Beale, backed by the carrier USS Randolph, off Cuba on 27 October 1962; that it carried one nuclear-tipped torpedo with roughly the yield of the Hiroshima bomb (10kt) and had been out of radio contact with Moscow for days; that US destroyers dropped signalling practice depth charges intended to force it to surface, not to sink it, which the exhausted crew inside did not know; that launching the torpedo needed unanimous agreement from B-59's three most senior officers (Savitsky, political officer Maslennikov, and detachment Chief of Staff Vasily Arkhipov), a requirement unique to B-59 among the four boats because Arkhipov's rank as detachment commander meant his consent was also needed, where the other three subs needed only two signatures; and that Arkhipov alone refused and persuaded Savitsky to surface instead. Also flags that naval intelligence officer Vadim Orlov's account of Savitsky's exact spoken words has itself been 'described as controversial,' which this topic deliberately does not quote.
